narrative:
The model predicted a 73% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with not passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.20 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not nearly enough to offset the much larger negative impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 31 (versus an accepted-student average of 37) and lower-middle family income also contributed to the risk, though less strongly. Full-time study plans aligned with the majority of successful applicants and did not hurt your chances.

To improve your prospects, focus on raising your class standing in the coming year and consider retaking the LSAT. Strengthening these two areas would most directly address the factors that led to this rejection. (218 words)
